title: Cloud hosting deals publish one billing term, not three
description: A source-linked term matrix for cloud hosting deals: which billing periods the provider actually prints, how each headline monthly figure is derived, and which cells stay blank.
answer: Every headline per-month price on a cloud hosting deal page is a 48-month prepaid amount divided by 48. For the entry cloud plan the provider prints $7.99/mo with a $383.52 upfront total and a $25.99/mo renewal rate, and all three belong to the same 48-month term. No 12-month and no 24-month price is printed for that plan on the pages checked, even though the provider's own pricing FAQ refers to an annual cloud hosting plan, so two of the three columns in a term comparison are blank rather than cheaper. Until a term is printed beside the number, treat any per-month figure as a multi-year prepaid commitment.
unique_note: This guide adds a term matrix assembled only from figures the provider prints. Sourced facts are the quoted prices, totals, renewal rates, term labels and the provider's own division rule. Clearly labelled derived arithmetic is limited to two things: the multiplication and division that reproduce each printed figure from the printed monthly rate and term, and the percentage each off badge implies. Nothing is converted between currencies, carried over from another plan, or estimated; cells with no published value are left blank.

sections.heading: The term is printed, and on the cloud plans it is 48 months
sections.body:
The pricing page renders a term control whose selected value reads '48 months plan'. The cloud hosting page answers its own plan-cost question with three figures, each tied to that same term: 'Cloud Startup - $7.99/month for the 48-month plan', 'Cloud Professional - $15.99/month for the 48-month plan' and 'Cloud Enterprise - $29.99/month for the 48-month plan'.

The pricing cards state the term as a total rather than a rate. For the entry cloud plan the card reads: 'Get 48 months for $383.52 (regular price $1,343.52). Renews at $25.99/mo.' The cloud hosting page's plan slider carries the matching renewal line: 'For 48-month term. $25.99/mo when you renew'.

Both pages also print the rule that connects the rate to the total. The pricing page and the VPS page say: 'All plans are paid upfront. The monthly rate reflects the total plan price divided by the number of months in your plan.' The cloud hosting page says: 'The price displayed is the monthly rate excluding applicable taxes. The total price for the plan to be paid upfront at checkout includes the monthly rate multiplied by the number of months in your plan, along with any applicable taxes.'

sections.heading: The term matrix: one column has numbers, two are blank
sections.body:
Using only what the checked pages print, the term matrix for the entry cloud plan looks like this.
12-month term: no price published. The pricing FAQ asks 'How do I register the free domain included with annual hosting plans?' and answers that the free 12-month domain applies to 'every annual managed hosting for WordPress, cloud hosting, or Website Builder plan', so an annual cloud hosting plan is named on the site, but no annual cloud hosting price is printed on the pages checked.
24-month term: no price published for the cloud plans. The only 24-month term found on the pricing page belongs to a different plan line, whose card reads 'For 24-month term. $49/mo when you renew'.
48-month term: published. $7.99/mo, an upfront total of $383.52, a regular price of $1,343.52, and a renewal rate of $25.99/mo.

The served HTML carries the 48-month figures and no other term's numbers, so a three-term comparison cannot be assembled from these pages. Following the gap's own instruction, the unpublished cells are recorded as unavailable rather than estimated.

sections.heading: Derived: the printed totals are the printed monthly rates multiplied by 48
sections.body:
This part is arithmetic on the provider's own printed numbers, not a provider statement.
$7.99 x 48 = $383.52, which is the printed upfront total, exactly.
$27.99 x 48 = $1,343.52, which is the printed regular price, exactly. The regular price is therefore a 48-month amount at the regular monthly rate, not a monthly rate itself.
$25.99 x 48 = $1,247.52, the 48-month value of the printed renewal rate.

The same pattern holds on the other two cards on the same page: $2.99 x 48 = $143.52 against a regular price of $575.52, and $3.99 x 48 = $191.52 against a regular price of $911.52. Every printed total divides back to a whole-cent monthly rate, so no rounding or estimation was needed to reproduce them.

sections.heading: Derived: what an off badge actually compares
sections.body:
Also arithmetic, and also derived rather than stated.
The entry cloud plan: 1 - (7.99 / 27.99) = 71.5%, which matches the '71% off' badge on the pricing page and the 'SAVE 71%' badge on the cloud hosting page.
The cheapest shared plan: 1 - (2.99 / 11.99) = 75.1%, matching its '75% off' badge.
The middle shared plan: 1 - (3.99 / 18.99) = 79.0%, matching its 'Special offer - 79% off' badge.
The Agency plan on the same pricing page: 1 - (29 / 69) = 58.0%, matching its 'SAVE 58%' badge.

Two conclusions follow. First, the badge is a ratio of two prices on the same basis, so it comes out the same whether the operands are monthly rates or 48-month totals; it carries no information about the length of the commitment. Second, on the cloud and shared cards both operands are 48-month amounts, so a badge reading 71% off describes a discount on a four-year prepaid total rather than on a monthly invoice.

sections.heading: The site normalizes renewal to two different horizons
sections.body:
The renewal line is not written against a single horizon across the provider's own pages.
The cloud hosting page writes it as a 48-month term: 'For 48-month term. $25.99/mo when you renew'.
The VPS page writes the same kind of line as a two-year term. Its cards read $6.49/mo with 'Renews at $11.99/mo for 2 years. Cancel anytime.', $8.99/mo with 'Renews at $14.99/mo for 2 years. Cancel anytime.', $12.99/mo with 'Renews at $28.99/mo for 2 years. Cancel anytime.' and $25.99/mo with 'Renews at $49.99/mo for 2 years. Cancel anytime.'
The Agency card on the pricing page writes it as a 24-month term.

Two years and 24 months describe the same span, so the cloud line is the outlier: it states its renewal against a four-year horizon while the other lines state theirs against two years. A reader comparing renewal rates across these pages is comparing different commitment lengths, and neither page says so.

sections.heading: A five-step check before comparing two cloud hosting deals
sections.body:
1. Find the term label before the price. On these pages the label is a select value reading '48 months plan' or a line reading 'for the 48-month plan', not the word 'month'.
2. Multiply the monthly rate by the term to get the money you actually commit, because the provider states that the monthly rate is the total divided by the months in the plan.
3. Decide whether the regular price in the card is a monthly rate or a term total. Here it is a 48-month total, which is why the badge reaches 71%.
4. Read the renewal line's own horizon, not just its number. On the same site that horizon is written as 48 months on the cloud page and 2 years on the VPS page.
5. Leave unpublished terms blank. A term with no printed price is unknown, not cheap.

sections.heading: What is still unknown
sections.body: The checked pages do not print a 12-month or a 24-month price for the cloud plans, a tax-inclusive checkout total, an exchange rate, or an end date for the rotating offer. The regular price is printed inside the 48-month sentence but is not separately labelled as a rate or as a total. None of these values is estimated here.

title: What is actually free in a cloud hosting deal, and for how long
description: A source-linked matrix of the extras bundled into a cloud hosting deal: the duration printed on each one, the single value the provider puts on any of them, and the refund clock the provider's own policy applies to each.
answer: Five extras are bundled into the cloud hosting deal card: a free domain, unlimited SSL, 15 AI Builder credits, unlimited mailboxes, and an included CDN. Only two of them print a duration - "Free domain for 1 year" and "Unlimited mailboxes per website - free for 1 year". One is labelled a "one-time gift". Two of them, unlimited SSL and the included CDN, print no boundary at all. The same free domain is then described with four different scopes on four provider pages: "for 1 year" on the deal card, "a free domain" with no duration in the cloud FAQ, "the free 12-month domain name included with every annual managed hosting for WordPress, cloud hosting, or Website Builder plan" in the pricing FAQ, and "included for one year with eligible annual plans" on the domains page - while the plan being sold is printed as a 48-month term. The refund policy then applies a shorter clock to the bundle than to the hosting: hosting may be refunded only if cancelled within 30 days of the transaction, but a new domain registration only if the refund is started within 96 hours of the registration, and "Domain Name Renewals" and "Privacy Protection" sit on the list of products not available for refunds - even though the pricing table prints "WHOIS privacy protection value $9.99" beside the same plans. No page read for this guide prices the bundled domain or the bundled mailboxes after the free year.
unique_note: Sourced facts on this page are the quoted lines, durations, values, windows and lists printed on the provider's own pages, each linked below. Clearly labelled derived arithmetic is limited to five things: the item counts inside the bundle block; the conversion of the 30-day, 96-hour and 168-hour windows into hours and the day on which the hosting and domain windows stop overlapping; the fourfold spread between the two readings of the printed $9.99 WHOIS value over a 48-month term; the count of 87 suffixes printed in the refund policy's ccTLD list; and the $19.98 difference between the two first-year .com figures printed on the domains page. No price, discount, traffic, ranking, click or index figure is estimated, and every cell the pages leave empty is reported as unstated rather than filled in.

sections.heading: The bundle the cloud deal card prints, item by item
sections.body:
The Cloud Startup card on the cloud hosting page prints its price and then this block of bundled extras, quoted as published:
Free domain for 1 year; Unlimited SSL FREE; 15 vibe coding credits (one-time gift) FREE; Unlimited mailboxes per website - free for 1 year FREE; Managed hosting for WordPress, WooCommerce, and Web Apps; CDN included; Dedicated IP address; Priority 24/7 expert support; 30-Day money-back guarantee; AI SEO ready

Two lines in that block carry a printed duration: the domain, "for 1 year", and the mailboxes, "free for 1 year". One line carries a different kind of limit: the AI Builder credits are "15" and a "one-time gift". Two of the bundled items, "Unlimited SSL" and "CDN included", print no period of any kind even though the domain and the mailboxes sitting beside them do. The dedicated IP address is listed without a FREE badge at all, so it reads as a plan feature rather than a promotional extra.

The same card's small print says the displayed figure is the monthly rate excluding applicable taxes and that the upfront total is that monthly rate multiplied by the number of months in the plan, which the card prints as a 48-month term. Nothing in the bundle block says what any of the five items costs once its printed period ends, and nothing in the block attaches a value to any of them.

sections.heading: The same free domain is described with four different scopes
sections.body:
Four provider pages carry a sentence about the free domain, and no two of them are worded the same way.
Cloud hosting deal card: "Free domain for 1 year"
Cloud hosting FAQ: "Every cloud hosting package includes a free domain, free SSL certificates, free domain-based emails, and 24/7 priority support."
Pricing FAQ: "To activate the free 12-month domain name included with every annual managed hosting for WordPress, cloud hosting, or Website Builder plan ..."
Domains page: "A free domain is included for one year with eligible annual plans."

Three of the four attach a duration of one year or 12 months; the cloud FAQ attaches none and instead folds the domain in with SSL, email and support as things the package "includes". Two of the four attach an eligibility condition - "annual" in the pricing FAQ, "eligible annual plans" on the domains page - while the plan those sentences would apply to is sold on the card as a 48-month term. None of the pages read for this guide states whether a 48-month cloud plan is one of the plans those eligibility sentences mean, so the one cell a reader would want to fill in stays empty.

sections.heading: The bundle's refund clock is shorter than the hosting's
sections.body: The refund policy sets one window for the plan and a different one for an item inside it. Its standard terms say: "Products purchased from Hostinger may be refunded only if canceled within 30 days of the date of the transaction." Its special terms for a domain say: "New registration of domain name: Refundable only if at the moment of initiation of the refund both the following conditions are met: (i) domain name refund is initiated within 96 hours from such domain name registration and (ii) more than 24 hours have passed from the moment of initiation of last refund of any other domain name registration."\n\nThe two windows are not close in size. Thirty days is 720 hours, so the 96-hour domain window is 13.3% of the hosting window and closes 624 hours, or 26 days, earlier. For a .br registration the policy prints a longer domain window of 168 hours, which is 7 days, still well inside the hosting's 30. The policy also prints a separate rule for a domain that was never activated: "Non-activated domain name: Refundable only if the domain name has not been activated and the cancellation is requested within the applicable 30-day refund period from the date of payment." The document does not say which of its two clauses governs a domain that has been registered but not yet activated.

sections.heading: Eighty-seven domain suffixes where a registration cannot be refunded at all
sections.body: The same special-terms section closes with a list introduced by this sentence: "The following ccTLD registries DO NOT permit refunds upon cancellation." The list is printed as a single run of suffixes, and it contains 87 entries. It mixes top-level suffixes with their sub-variants - for example .uk is printed together with .co.uk, .org.uk and .me.uk, and .pl with .com.pl, .net.pl, .info.pl and .biz.pl - and it includes widely used extensions such as .de, .eu, .fr, .it, .nl, .se, .us, .in, .jp, .au, .ca, .ch and .ai.\n\nFor a buyer reading the deal card this matters because the card prints one undivided promise, "Free domain for 1 year", with no hint that the extension chosen changes what happens if the plan is cancelled. The count of 87 is derived by counting the suffixes printed in that one sentence; the sentence itself is quoted, not paraphrased.

sections.heading: The one value the provider prints for a bundled item: WHOIS privacy protection, $9.99
sections.body: The pricing page's feature comparison lists, for every cloud plan, the row "WHOIS privacy protection value $9.99". It is the only figure in the bundle neighbourhood of any page read for this guide that puts a number on a bundled extra. The numeral is printed with no period attached, so the same text supports two readings over the 48-month term the card sells: $9.99 once, or $9.99 for each of four years, which is $39.96. The page does not say which one it means, and the two readings differ fourfold.\n\nThe refund policy pulls the other way. "Privacy Protection" appears on its list of products not available for refunds, in the same list as "Domain Name Renewals", "Redemption Fees" and "Domain Name Transfers (if the transfer is successful)". So an item the pricing table values at $9.99 is an item the policy says cannot be refunded. The same list also names "Hostinger AI Builder credits", which the deal card badges "FREE" and describes as a "one-time gift".

sections.heading: The free domain is claimed, not granted, and that moves the clock
sections.body: The pricing FAQ describes the free domain as an action rather than an automatic inclusion: "simply log in to your dashboard, click on the Claim domain button, find your perfect domain, and register it." The refund policy then measures the domain's clock from a different event than the hosting's: the domain window runs "within 96 hours from such domain name registration", while the hosting window runs "within 30 days of the date of the transaction".\n\nIf the claim is what starts the domain clock, the two windows do not stay nested. Claiming on day 25 of a 30-day hosting window leaves 5 days, or 120 hours, of hosting window, and the domain's own 96-hour window closes on day 29 - one day before the hosting window does. Claim on day 26 and the two close together. Claim on or after day 27 and the domain's 96-hour window extends past the end of the hosting's 30-day window. The deal card prints the 30-day money-back guarantee and the free domain in the same block without noting that the two are measured from different starting points.

sections.heading: The same bundle line appears on other plans with different refund rules
sections.body: The free domain is not a cloud-only line. The VPS page prints "Free domain for 1 year" in its feature list, and the shared hosting and WordPress hosting cards print "Domain - free for 1 year". The quantity attached to the mailboxes is not consistent across them: the cloud card says "Unlimited mailboxes per website - free for 1 year", while the WordPress page's FAQ says managed WooCommerce plans come with "a free domain name, unlimited free SSL certificates, 100 free email addresses, and free CDN".\n\nThe refund rules behind those identical-looking lines differ too. The refund policy's standard list reads "Hosting (all plans, except first payment after Free Trial and all VPS hosting plans)" and then names "VPS (except upgrades)" and "KVM VPS (except upgrades)" as items available under those same standard terms, while a separate special clause adds a further condition for VPS: the refund must be initiated "within 30 days of the date of the transaction of that specific VPS hosting plan" and "more than 180 days" must have passed since the last VPS refund. Read together with the domain clause, the cooldown printed between two refunds is 24 hours for a domain registration and 180 days for a VPS plan.

sections.heading: What the pages read for this guide do not state
sections.body:
These cells are empty on every page read for this guide. They are listed as unstated rather than filled in:
The price of the bundled domain after the free year. The domains page says only that "Standard renewal rates apply after year one", with no number.
The price of the bundled mailboxes after the free year.
Whether a bundled free domain is valued, deducted or clawed back when the hosting plan itself is refunded. The policy states a rule for a domain bought as a product; it does not state how a bundled one is treated.
Which domain extensions are eligible for the free domain.
Whether the 96-hour new-registration rule is the clause that applies to a bundled free domain, or whether the 30-day non-activated rule applies instead.
Whether the $9.99 WHOIS privacy protection value is a yearly figure or a one-off.
Whether a 48-month cloud plan counts as an "annual" plan for the eligibility sentences in the pricing FAQ and on the domains page.

One further figure sits nearby without being part of the bundle: the domains page prints ".com" at "$19.99" beside "$0.01 /1st yr", with the note "*Applicable when you choose a 3-year term. Standard renewal rates apply after year one." The difference between the two printed first-year figures is $19.98, and the 3-year term in that note is a third different term length from the 48-month cloud term.

sections.heading: How to read a bundle when you compare cloud hosting deals
sections.body:
The deal card treats the bundle as a list of features. Reading it as a list of durations gives a different picture, and the provider's own documents supply everything needed to do that:
Separate the items that print a period from the items that do not. On this card that is two against two, with one labelled one-time.
Find the claim step. If the item has to be claimed, its clock may start at the claim rather than at checkout.
Check the refund rule per item, not per plan. The plan's 30 days does not carry over to a new domain registration.
Count an item at a value only where a page prints one, and treat a value printed without a period as a value with an unknown period.
Treat a "free" badge with no duration as a statement about the term you are buying, not as a permanent entitlement.

All figures quoted here were read from the provider's own pages on 2026-09-28, and the sources are linked below so they can be re-checked. Prices, discounts and bundled extras on these pages rotate, so a figure quoted here may not be the figure on the page today.

title: Cloud hosting deals print four different backup promises
description: Plan cards badge backups as weekly, daily, daily-and-on-demand, or free weekly. Only the knowledge base states the schedule, the retention window, the tier gate and the exclusions.
answer: Four different backup promises are printed across the provider's own plan pages. The Premium card says "Free weekly backups". The Unlimited card says "Daily backups + easy data restore". The Cloud Startup card says "Daily and on demand backups". The VPS page prints "Free weekly backups" three times and never prints "daily backups", while the cloud hosting page prints "daily backups" once in its benefits line. Only the knowledge base states the rule behind those badges: "we provide weekly backups for all of our hosting plans, as well as daily backups for Web Business and greater hosting plans". The same article adds that on a Web Single or Premium plan daily backups are something you "purchase", that the purchased daily backups are "stored for the last 7 days" and then "automatically deleted", and that VPS daily backups are kept as "2 most recent daily backups and 2 most recent weekly backups". Manual backups are a "Business or greater" tool capped at "once every 24 hours". Six third-party backup tools covering seven folder paths are excluded from every backup, and the provider states the exclusion cannot be turned off.
unique_note: Sourced facts on this page are the quoted backup strings, schedules, retention windows, tier names, purchase conditions, cadences and folder paths printed on the provider's own pages, each linked below. Clearly labelled derived arithmetic is limited to five things: the count of four distinct backup strings printed across the plan pages; the count of three "Free weekly backups" badges and zero "daily backups" strings on the VPS page; the count of six backup tools and seven folder paths in the exclusion table; the comparisons drawn from published figures only - the 3.5x difference between the published 7-day web retention window and the published 2-day VPS retention window, and the roughly 1/209th share of a 48-month term that a 7-day window covers; and the observation that the published manual cadence of one backup per 24 hours is the same frequency as the published automated daily schedule. No price, retention window, schedule, backup size or restore time is estimated anywhere on this page; cells the provider does not publish are reported as unstated.

sections.heading: The four backup strings the plan cards print
sections.body:
Backup wording on this provider changes with the plan tier, not with the product. The pricing page publishes three plan cards and each carries a different string.

Premium, printed at $2.99/mo with "Get 48 months for $143.52 (regular price $575.52)": "Free weekly backups". The same card prints 3 websites, 20 GB SSD storage and a domain free for 1 year.

Unlimited, printed at $3.99/mo with "Get 48 months for $191.52 (regular price $911.52)": "Daily backups + easy data restore". The same card prints unlimited websites and 50 GB NVMe storage.

Cloud Startup, printed at $7.99/mo with "Get 48 months for $383.52 (regular price $1,343.52)": "Daily and on demand backups". The same card prints unlimited websites and 100 GB NVMe storage.

That is four distinct backup strings once the VPS page is added. On the VPS page the plan strip prints "Free weekly backups" three times and the string "daily backups" appears zero times. The cloud hosting page does the opposite: it prints "daily backups" once, in its benefits line - "Stable and secure 99.9% uptime, daily backups, and DDoS protection so busy days stay online and client data stays put" - and prints no weekly backup promise at all.

The pricing page's own "Compare our plans" block lists a row labelled "Daily backups" among its top features. The per-plan values for that row could not be attributed from the served markup, so this guide reports none of them.

sections.heading: Only the knowledge base states the schedule, and it says weekly
sections.body:
One provider page states a schedule for backups: the knowledge base article on activating daily backups. Its opening line carries the rule that none of the plan cards print.

"At Hostinger, we provide weekly backups for all of our hosting plans, as well as daily backups for Web Business and greater hosting plans."

Read against the plan cards, that sentence makes the badges tier statements rather than product statements. Weekly is the baseline for every hosting plan, so "Free weekly backups" on the VPS strip and on the Premium card is the default rather than a downgrade. Daily is an entitlement that begins at a named tier, and the tier the knowledge base names is "Web Business and greater" while the plan the pricing page prints is called "Unlimited".

No page read for this guide states that those two names refer to the same tier, so this guide does not merge them. The cloud hosting page's "daily backups" line is therefore a tier claim it does not qualify, and a buyer reading only that line has no way to tell whether the promise applies to the cloud plan on the page or to a higher tier on a different page.

sections.heading: On the lower plans, daily backups are a purchase rather than a feature
sections.body:
The knowledge base article is explicit that daily backups on the cheaper plans are bought.

"If you have a Web Single or Premium plan and want to have daily backups, you can easily purchase this feature."

The flow it describes is a dashboard purchase: "Websites -> Dashboard", then "Backups under the Files menu", then "the Add Daily Backups button", then "Select the duration and payment method". Two things follow from that wording. First, the daily-backup entitlement on a lower plan has a duration the buyer chooses rather than a duration the plan fixes. Second, no price for it appears on any page read for this guide - the figure sits behind the dashboard flow.

The article then prints the alternative route: "Alternatively, you can get daily backups by upgrading your hosting plan to Business Web Hosting or above." So the same outcome is reachable two ways on a lower plan, a separate purchase or a tier upgrade, and neither price is printed beside the backup badge on the plan card.

The VPS route has the same shape. The VPS section of the same article directs the reader to open "Snapshots & Backups", then "click Upgrade under Daily Backups", then "Select the duration and payment method". A VPS buyer who reads only the deal page sees "Free weekly backups" and no indication that daily copies are a separate priced upgrade.

sections.heading: Two retention windows are published, and neither covers the included daily backups
sections.body:
Retention is the part of a backup promise that decides whether a copy is still there when it is needed, and this provider publishes two numbers for it.

For a purchased daily backup on Web Single or Premium: "Daily backups are created and stored for the last 7 days. After that time, they are automatically deleted." The same block adds "Manual deletion of these backups is not supported."

For a purchased VPS daily backup: "Daily backups are created and stored for 2 most recent daily backups and 2 most recent weekly backups. After that time, they are automatically deleted."

Derived from those two printed figures: the published web window is 3.5 times the published VPS daily window, 7 days against 2 days. On the published VPS rule a buyer holds at most four restore points, two daily and two weekly, while the published web rule allows up to seven daily copies.

Derived: the 7-day window is also short against the term the plan is sold on. A 48-month term is about 1,461 days, so the published retention window covers roughly 1/209th of the period the customer has prepaid.

What is not published matters as much. The retention window for the daily backups that the higher tiers include is not stated on any page read for this guide - the 7-day figure is printed in the section about the feature bought on Single and Premium, not in a section about the entitlement that Business and greater receive. The retention window for the baseline weekly backups is not stated either. Both cells are left blank here rather than filled with the nearest available number.

sections.heading: A manual backup is a Business-or-greater tool, capped at one every 24 hours
sections.body:
The second backup control is manual, and it is tier-gated in the provider's own words.

"At Hostinger, if your hosting plan is Business or greater, you can use the Backup tool to manually create backups of all the files and databases on your hosting plan."

The same page caps the cadence: "You can generate a new backup using this method once every 24 hours. If your hosting plan does not include this feature, consider upgrading it." It also sets expectations on time - the process "can take a few minutes to a few hours, depending on the number and size of files and databases in your hosting plan" - and notes that the Manage Backups view shows "the date of the last backup" and "the date of the next backup".

Derived from the two published cadences: a manual backup is limited to one per 24 hours, which is the same frequency as an automated daily backup. The difference between the two routes is who triggers the copy, not how often the provider permits one to be taken. A Business-or-greater customer can therefore reach the daily cadence without buying the daily add-on, while a customer below Business reaches the manual route not at all and reaches daily backups only by paying for the add-on or by upgrading a tier.

sections.heading: Six backup tools and seven folders are excluded from every backup, with no opt-out
sections.body:
The most consequential limit is published on a separate knowledge base page, and it is neither a schedule nor a window: certain files are never in the backup at all.

"Hostinger automatically creates regular backups of your website files and databases so you can restore your data if an emergency occurs. To keep these automated processes fast, reliable, and optimal in size, Hostinger leaves out one specific type of file: backups created by third-party WordPress backup plugins."

The page prints the excluded paths in a table: All-in-One WP Migration stores archives in wp-content/ai1wm-backups; UpdraftPlus in wp-content/updraft; WPvivid Backup in wp-content/wpvividbackups and wp-content/uploads/wpvividbackups; Duplicator (Lite) in wp-content/backups-dup-lite; Duplicator Pro in wp-content/backups-dup-pro; and other backup tools in wp-content/wp-snapshots. Derived from that printed table: six backup tools, seven folder paths.

The consequence is stated twice. On whether the rule can be switched off: "Can I turn this backup exclusion off? No." On recovering an excluded archive: "I need a plugin-made backup file that was excluded - can Hostinger recover it? No. Because Hostinger backups do not store these archive folders, they cannot be recovered through Hostinger dashboard."

The page anchors the rule in the provider's terms as well: "This is also described in our Terms of Service: backups created by third-party software, plugins, or services may be excluded from Hostinger's backup, retention, and restore processes." It names the plans in scope as "An active Hostinger web, cloud, or agency hosting plan", so the exclusion reaches cloud plans rather than shared hosting alone.

What remains covered is listed too - WordPress core files, themes and plugins, the uploads directory and database tables - and the provider's own summary is that the "actual website - pages, images, themes, plugins, and database - is still fully backed up", because the excluded items are copies made by other backup tools rather than live site files. The practical reading is narrow but real: a restore brings the site back, and the plugin-made archives a customer may have been counting on do not come with it.

sections.heading: The provider's limits table counts MySQL backup sizes, not backup schedules
sections.body: The provider publishes a parameters and limits table for its hosting plans, which is the natural place to look for a backup limit. Its only backup-adjacent rows concern MySQL data rather than the backup routine: "MySQL max backup size (MB)", printed as 5,120 for the first group of plans, then 10,240, 20,480, 46,080 and 46,080 for the next group, and 46,080 for the cloud group.\n\nThose rows govern how large a MySQL export or import may be. They say nothing about when a backup is taken, how long it is kept, who may trigger one manually, or what is left out of it. The table and the backup pages answer different questions, and a buyer comparing deals who reads only the table learns a number that sounds like a backup limit while missing every term that decides whether a restore is possible.

sections.heading: What the pages read for this guide do not state
sections.body:
- The retention window for the daily backups included with Business-or-greater plans. The published 7-day figure appears in the section about the feature bought on Web Single and Premium.

- The retention window for the baseline weekly backups, on any plan.

- The price of the daily-backup add-on for Web Single, Premium or VPS. The knowledge base describes choosing "the duration and payment method" but prints no figure.

- Whether the plan the pricing page calls "Unlimited" is the same tier the knowledge base calls "Web Business and greater". No page read for this guide states that the two names match.

- Whether the excluded plugin folders are skipped on VPS plans. The exclusion page names web, cloud and agency hosting plans.

- The size of a backup on any plan, and any restore-time commitment. The knowledge base gives a range for creating a backup but prints no target or maximum for a restore.

sections.heading: How to read a backup badge when you compare cloud hosting deals
sections.body:
Five checks turn a badge into a term.

1. Find the schedule, not the word. "Backups" and "daily backups" are different promises, and on this provider the schedule is printed in the knowledge base rather than on the plan card.

2. Ask whether the schedule is included or bought. If daily backups are an add-on on the plan under consideration, the badge describes an option rather than the plan.

3. Find the retention window and match it to the product. The published web window and the published VPS window are different figures from the same provider.

4. Check what is excluded before relying on the backup. A permanently excluded folder makes an independent off-server copy mandatory, and the provider's own advice points the same way: configure third-party plugins to "send its backups to external storage - such as Google Drive, Dropbox, or Amazon S3".

5. Check the tier gate on manual backups. If the manual tool starts above the plan being bought, an on-demand copy is not available at all.

Derived from the published rules: the shortest retention window this provider publishes is the VPS daily window of 2 daily copies plus 2 weekly copies, and the longest prepaid commitment it sells is a 48-month term. A 7-day window against a 48-month term is the kind of mismatch worth pricing before purchase, because the backup that matters is the one still stored on the day something breaks.

title: Cloud hosting deals sell a server location you cannot see until checkout
description: The plan pages print a location slogan and name no country. The provider's own list names twelve places for web and cloud, and the rules for changing that choice differ by product.
answer: The provider's own plan pages advertise where your site will live without naming a single country. The pricing page's plan comparison carries a row reading “Global data centers”. The cloud hosting page carries a block headed “Data centers worldwide”. The VPS page prints “Data centers worldwide” twice in its feature strip. None of the three pages names a country, a city or a region for the plan it is selling, and the cloud hosting page's eight-question FAQ never mentions a data centre or a server location. The names are published in the provider's own location article instead. For web and cloud hosting it lists ten countries — France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom; India, Indonesia and Malaysia; the USA, broken out into Phoenix, Boston and Asheville; and Brazil. For VPS it lists nine, dropping the Netherlands and Asheville. For Agency hosting it lists five places, and for legacy cPanel hosting five countries with no cities. Whether you can change that choice, and what changing it costs you, is also published elsewhere and differs by product. Web and cloud hosting can change server location “once every 30 days”, and a transfer “can take up to 4 hours” during which the hosting panel is locked and the hosting IP changes. Agency hosting plans “do not support changing the server location after purchase”. A VPS location is “fixed after initial setup”, and moving means reinstalling, which “will permanently delete all existing data, including backups and snapshots”. For websites built with AI Builder, “the server location cannot be changed”. The provider also states that “data center availability is subject to change without prior notice” and that the only authoritative list is the one displayed in its dashboard during setup or a server transfer.
unique_note: Sourced facts on this page are the location strings printed on the provider's plan pages, the place names and product-by-product lists in the provider's location article, the change cadence, transfer duration, panel lock, IP change, DNS propagation, temporary-domain and subdomain rules in the provider's transfer articles, the irreversibility statements for Agency, VPS and AI Builder, the availability and revertibility caveats, the renewable-electricity statement and the IP-database delay, each linked below. Clearly labelled derived arithmetic is limited to counts and one ratio drawn from published figures only: the count of six region tabs and the count of one tab rendered with place names and five served without panel content, read from the served markup; the count of three names in the rendered panel and of twelve named places in the web and cloud list, with nine of those twelve not appearing on the cloud hosting page; the count of ten countries for web and cloud, ten named places for VPS, five for Agency and five for legacy cPanel; the count of two places the VPS list drops from the web and cloud list; the count of six widget region tabs against the four continents the web and cloud list spans; and the ratio of a transfer of up to 4 hours to the 720 hours in the published 30-day minimum interval between changes. No price, latency figure, performance number, location count or transfer duration is estimated anywhere on this page; cells the provider does not publish are reported as unstated.

sections.heading: The location strings the plan pages actually print
sections.body:
Location is sold as a feature on every plan page, and on every plan page it is sold as a slogan rather than a place. The pricing page lists “Global data centers” as a plan feature row, sitting between the “99.9% uptime guarantee” row and the “Free automatic website migration” row in the comparison of the three cloud plans. The cloud hosting page devotes a whole block to it, headed “Data centers worldwide”, with the line “Select a data center location close to your target audience for faster loading times, at all times.” The VPS page repeats the same two words “Data centers worldwide” twice, once per copy of its feature strip, and adds a sentence further down: “Choose a server location close to your audience to boost loading speeds. We have data centers across North America, Europe, Asia, and South America.” 

 That sentence is the closest any plan page comes to describing the offer, and it describes it by continent. Four continents are named. Zero countries and zero cities are named. The same page carries a widget whose visible label is “Recommended server location:” followed by “Checking...” — the recommendation is produced in the browser, and the served markup publishes no recommendation at all. 

 The cloud hosting page's FAQ runs eight questions about what cloud hosting is, who should buy it, how migration works, what it costs and how to upgrade. The words “data center” and “server location” do not appear in any of the answers.

sections.heading: What the region widget renders, and what it leaves to JavaScript
sections.body: The cloud hosting page's location block is a tabbed region selector. Six region tabs are served: North America, South America, Europe, South Africa, Asia and Australia. Only the first tab is rendered with place names in the HTML the server sends. Its panel is labelled “Locations in North America” and lists three names: Arizona, Massachusetts and New York. The other five tabs — South America, Europe, South Africa, Asia and Australia — are served as buttons with no panel content behind them, so the place names for five of the six regions exist only after JavaScript runs. \n\n The block also carries one chip, “Locations with both Data Centers and CDNs”. That chip is a label on the list rather than a definition of it: it implies that some entries in the widget are data-centre locations, some are CDN locations, and some are both, without saying which entry is which. A reader who only sees the served page cannot tell whether Arizona, Massachusetts and New York are data centres, CDN points of presence, or both.

sections.heading: The published location list, product by product
sections.body:
The provider's location article is the page that names places, and it names a different set for each product. 

 Web and cloud hosting: Europe — France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. Asia — India, Indonesia and Malaysia. North America — the USA, broken into Phoenix, Boston and Asheville. South America — Brazil. That is ten countries and twelve named places. 

 Agency hosting: Germany (Frankfurt), India (Mumbai), the USA (Phoenix and Boston), Brazil and the United Kingdom. That is five named places, and the same article states that changing the server location after the initial setup is not yet available for Agency plans. 

 VPS hosting, including KVM and Game Panel: Europe — France, Germany, Lithuania and the United Kingdom. Asia — India, Indonesia and Malaysia. North America — the USA (Phoenix and Boston). South America — Brazil. That is ten named places, and the article is explicit about what was removed: servers in the Netherlands and in Asheville are available for web and cloud plans only, not for VPS. 

 Legacy cPanel hosting: Lithuania, the United Kingdom, India, the USA and Brazil — five countries, no cities. 

 The same article names three locations that it does not put in any of those lists, because they are CDN rather than data-centre locations: Johannesburg (South Africa), Japan and Sydney (Australia).

sections.heading: Where the page and the list do not line up
sections.body:
Set the cloud hosting page's rendered panel beside the location list for the same product and the two do not describe the same set. The page names three US states: Arizona, Massachusetts and New York. The list names twelve places, three of them in the USA: Phoenix, Boston and Asheville. Two of the three page names line up with two of the three list names — Phoenix is in Arizona and Boston is in Massachusetts. The third page name, New York, does not appear in the web and cloud list at all, and the list names Asheville in its place. 

 The count of regions does not line up either. The widget offers six region tabs; the web and cloud location list spans four continents — Europe, Asia, North America and South America. The two extra tabs are South Africa and Australia, and those are exactly the regions the location article classifies as CDN rather than data-centre locations when it names Johannesburg and Sydney. 

 Counted as names rather than regions, nine of the twelve places the provider publishes for web and cloud hosting are not printed anywhere on the cloud hosting page itself. 

 This is a description of two provider-published pages, not a claim that either is wrong. The widget's own chip, “Locations with both Data Centers and CDNs”, shows that its list deliberately mixes two kinds of site, and the location article is the page that separates them. What a buyer cannot do is reconcile the two from the pages alone: nothing on the cloud hosting page says which of its names is a data centre and which is a CDN edge.

sections.heading: Changing your mind has a published cadence
sections.body:
The location article says a location can be selected during initial setup and that an active web or cloud plan can be moved from the Plan Details page in the dashboard. The separate transfer article supplies the rule the location article omits: the server location can be changed once every 30 days. That is the only rate limit the provider publishes for the change, and it appears on neither the pricing page nor the cloud hosting page. 

 The same article publishes the cost in time. A server transfer can take up to 4 hours to complete, and during that window the hosting panel is locked to prevent changes, with an explicit instruction not to make any changes during the process because registrations, new content and orders made directly on the website may not be preserved after the transfer completes. 

 Derived from those two published figures: 30 days is 720 hours, so a transfer of up to 4 hours occupies about 0.6% of the shortest interval the provider allows between two changes. The provider publishes no monthly, annual or per-change price for a transfer, so the money cost of using that allowance is unstated.

sections.heading: Three products where the choice is not reversible
sections.body:
For three of the products in the location list, changing the location after purchase is either unsupported or destructive, and none of the three deal pages says so. 

 Agency hosting: the location article states that changing the server location after the initial setup is not yet available for Agency hosting plans, and the transfer article repeats that Agency plans do not support changing the server location after purchase — the location is chosen only when setting up a new Agency plan. The published alternative is to buy a second Agency plan in the wanted location and use the cloning feature to move the website across, which means paying for two plans rather than moving one. 

 VPS hosting: the location is fixed after it is selected during setup. The transfer article describes the workaround as reinstalling the VPS in a different location, and both the transfer article and the dedicated VPS relocation article state that reinstalling in a new location will permanently delete all existing data, including backups and snapshots, and that a full backup should be downloaded beforehand. The VPS page itself advertises free weekly backups and snapshots as a plan feature, and those are among the items the relocation article says are destroyed by the move. 

 AI Builder websites: the transfer article states that websites created with AI Builder have integrated CDN features by default and therefore the server location cannot be changed. The AI Builder location article explains the same thing from the other direction — the site's assets are served through the provider's own CDN, which it describes as the default and only CDN option for AI Builder sites. For those sites the location question is answered by removing the choice rather than by publishing one.

sections.heading: What a transfer does to your site, your IP and your DNS
sections.body:
The transfer article publishes a list of side effects that a location change carries, and none of them appears on a deal page. The hosting IP changes, and the provider emails the new value when the transfer finishes. A domain pointed at the provider by A record must have that record updated by hand; a domain pointed by nameservers is updated automatically. Any remote connection, API or script that depends on the IP must be updated manually too. 

 The website and email may temporarily stop working while the change propagates through DNS, which the article says takes a few hours to complete. A temporary domain of the form yoursite.hostingersite.com stops working after the transfer, so a site that has not yet been connected to its real domain needs that connection finished first or redone afterwards. Subdomains that use custom A records are not updated automatically even when the domain uses the provider's nameservers, and each of those A records has to be pointed at the new IP by hand. 

 Read together with the published cadence, the practical shape of the offer is this: the change is possible on web and cloud plans, at most once every 30 days, and each use of it carries an IP change, a locked panel for up to 4 hours, a DNS propagation window during which the site and email may not respond, and a manual DNS checklist. None of that appears beside the “Global data centers” row.

sections.heading: The provider's own caveat about the list
sections.body:
The location article ends its list with two notes that qualify everything above it. Data centre availability is subject to change without prior notice, and the final list of available locations is the one displayed in the provider's dashboard during the setup or server transfer process. Locations available during initial setup are subject to future capacity constraints, and a user who changes server location may be unable to revert to the original selection. 

 Two consequences follow from those sentences as published. The list on the location article is not a guarantee of what will be offered at checkout, by the provider's own statement. And a change is not necessarily reversible: the provider says a user may be unable to go back to the location they started in, which turns a change made for a temporary reason into a possibly permanent one. 

 The same article states a separate, non-technical commitment about the data centres themselves: all of the provider's data centres have their electricity use matched with 100% renewable electricity, achieved either by the provider or by its colocation partners through supply contracts and power purchase agreements, or through renewable electricity certificates including European Guarantees of Origin, North American Renewable Energy Certificates and International Renewable Energy Certificates. That claim is about the electricity behind the sites, not about where they are, and it is the only environmental statement the location article makes.

sections.heading: What remains unstated
sections.body:
Several cells a buyer would want are simply not published anywhere on the pages read for this article, and they are reported here as unstated rather than estimated. 

 There is no published price for a server transfer, so the cost of using the once-every-30-days allowance is unknown. There is no published latency figure, response-time target or performance guarantee tied to any named location, so the speed benefit the pages promise is not quantified. There is no published mapping from a plan tier to a subset of locations, so whether every cloud plan can reach every one of the twelve web and cloud places is unstated. There is no published number of data centres behind any single country. And there is no published statement reconciling the widget's third North American name with the location list's third US city. 

 One more cell is unstated for a different reason: the IP-location article explains that public IP lookup databases often show the wrong location for a provider's addresses, that the provider publishes a geofeed to correct this, and that public databases may take up to two months to catch up. So a third-party IP lookup is not a reliable way to check which location a plan was actually placed in — the provider's own dashboard is.

title: Cloud hosting deals call the purchase risk-free. The exit is 30 days, then the door closes
description: The deal page prints a 30-day money-back guarantee and calls the purchase risk-free. The provider's own terms make that a 30-day cancellation window, default the plan to auto-renewal for a term as long as the one you bought, and state that fees are otherwise non-refundable.
answer: The cloud hosting deal page prints a 30-day money-back guarantee five times and calls the purchase risk-free twice, but it never uses the words auto-renew or cancel. The provider's own terms define what that guarantee actually is. The refund policy states that products may be refunded only if canceled within 30 days of the date of the transaction, and the support article on cancelling a service adds that requesting a refund will result in the immediate termination of the service. So the 30 days is a cooling-off window on a purchase, not an open-ended trial, and using it ends the service at once. Outside those 30 days the contractual default is the opposite of risk-free: all fees for services are non-refundable unless the refund policy expressly says otherwise, and no page publishes any pro-rata return of the term you already paid. What you can do at any time is switch off auto-renewal, but that does not shorten the term. The support article is explicit that the service will remain active until its expiration date and is then automatically canceled and deleted from the account, and that there is no delete button or menu option in the dashboard for Hostinger services. Leave auto-renewal on instead and the terms renew the plan by default for a subsequent period equal in length to the one you just bought, at then-current fees, charged from 30 to 0 calendar days before the current term ends, with email notice that the provider describes as a right and not an obligation.
unique_note: Sourced facts in this article are quoted from pages the provider publishes: the cloud hosting deal page and the pricing page for what is advertised, the universal terms of service for the auto-renewal and refund clauses, the refund policy for eligibility, and four provider support articles for the mechanics of disabling auto-renewal, cancelling a service, upgrading, downgrading and buying a new plan instead of renewing. The derived figures are labelled as derived: the share of a 48-month term covered by a 30-day window, the day count used for that share, the position of the earliest renewal charge inside a 48-month term, the ratio between the printed promotional rate and the printed renewal rate, and the multiple between the 30-day refund window and the published 180-day VPS refund cooldown. No price, discount, value, count or timing that the provider does not print has been supplied, and where a number is not published, the article says so instead of estimating it.

sections.heading: What the deal page prints about leaving, and what it does not
sections.body:
The cloud hosting page is generous with the guarantee and silent on the mechanics. The phrase money-back appears five times in the served HTML and risk-free twice, including the line Get started in complete confidence. Our 30-day money-back guarantee means it's risk-free, and a second version further down the page promising that you can explore our services without risk.

The same page prints the rate you would pay afterwards, on the plan card itself: For 48-month term. $25.99/mo when you renew.

What the same page does not print is anything about the mechanism that makes that renewal happen. The string auto-renew appears zero times in the served HTML of the deal page, and the string cancel appears zero times as well. The pricing page is the same on the first count and different on the second: it prints Cancel anytime twice as a feature line beside the plan selector, and it prints auto-renew zero times. So the two pages a buyer is most likely to read advertise a guarantee and an anytime exit, and neither one uses the word that governs whether the plan renews.

sections.heading: The guarantee is a cancellation window, and cancelling means terminating
sections.body:
Three provider documents converge on the same reading. The legal refund policy states that products purchased from Hostinger may be refunded only if canceled within 30 days of the date of the transaction. The support article on cancelling a service states that requesting a refund will result in the immediate termination of the service. Section 16 of the universal terms of service states that requests and claims related to payments, including refunds, will be handled only if they are provided not later than within 30 calendar days of the date of purchase of the service.

Those three sentences describe one thing: a 30-day cooling-off period that ends the purchase, not a trial that can be ended whenever the buyer chooses. The support article also makes clear that the termination is not partial. Cancelling a hosting plan that came with a free email trial cancels the email trial with it, and the article advises upgrading to a paid mail plan first if the email is meant to survive.

This is the point the deal page's own wording skips. Risk-free is printed against a commitment whose only published exit is 30 days long.

sections.heading: What is inside the 30 days, and the shorter clocks within it
sections.body:
The refund policy summary lists what the 30-day window covers: new purchases and renewals of web, cloud, Agency, KVM VPS and Game Panel hosting plans; new purchases, renewals and upgrades for Hostinger Email and for Titan Email; and upgrades for web, cloud and Agency hosting plans. It also lists what the window never covers: domain name renewals, completed domain transfers, domain redemption fees, Google Workspace Email, VPS Control Panel licences, upgrades for KVM VPS and Game Panel plans, GPU and LLM products and Hostinger credits of any type, domain name registrations for most country-code TLDs, and any purchase made with cryptocurrency, tokens or digital assets.

One asymmetry is worth reading twice. An upgrade is refundable on web, cloud and Agency hosting, but upgrades for KVM VPS and Game Panel plans are excluded from the policy altogether. The same action is reversible on one product line and not on another.

Inside the 30 days there are also shorter clocks. New registrations on general TLDs such as .com, .net and .org are refundable only within 96 hours of registration, and domain transfers only if the transfer was unsuccessful and the refund is requested within 96 hours. Brazilian registrations get 7 days. If the refunded hosting plan included a free domain, the standard price of that domain may be deducted from the total refund amount, and the buyer keeps ownership of the domain for the remainder of its billing period - a price the deal page does not print anywhere. VPS plans carry an extra condition: after a VPS refund, a 180-day cooldown applies before another VPS refund is available, which is six times the length of the 30-day window itself, a multiple derived from the two published figures.

sections.heading: After day 30 the contract default is that nothing comes back
sections.body: The terms of service state the default plainly: all fees for services are non-refundable, even if the services are suspended, terminated or restricted in any other manner, or transferred prior to the end of the subscription period, unless the refund policy expressly specifies otherwise. The transferred case is worth noting, because it closes a route a buyer might assume exists: moving the service to another plan or another account before the term ends does not create a refund right.\n\nNor is there a published pro-rata. The same section states that the total amount of fees for the period the buyer selects is charged and paid upfront. On the 48-month term the deal page sells, the 30-day window covers one of 48 monthly instalments - about 2% of the term, a share derived from the two printed numbers - and roughly 30 days out of a 48-month period, which is about 1,461 days if the term includes a leap day, again derived rather than published. Whatever the remaining term is worth, no page offers to return it.

sections.heading: The lever you keep does not shorten the term
sections.body:
Disabling auto-renewal is available at any time, and the support article is unusually clear about what it does not do. It states that disabling auto-renewal does not affect the current service status and that the service will remain active until the expiration date. The companion article on cancelling a service repeats it and adds the ending: once auto-renewal is disabled, the service will remain active until its expiration date, and after that date the service will be automatically canceled and deleted from the account. The same article states that there is no delete button or menu option in the dashboard for Hostinger services, which is why the renewal switch is the only control on offer.

Two further limits sit on that switch. The article notes that disabling the feature does not refund or revert charges that have already been processed. And it notes that to change the billing cycle, auto-renewal must be enabled - so the setting that ends the deal is also the setting that must stay on if the buyer wants a different cycle.

The practical effect is that switching auto-renewal off is a decision about the next term, not about this one. It stops a future charge; it does not refund or shorten the term already paid for.

sections.heading: Auto-renewal is the default, and the next term is as long as this one
sections.body: Section 16 of the terms of service sets the frame. All paid services are provided on a subscription basis unless indicated otherwise, and by buying on that basis the buyer consents that services will be auto-renewed until the auto-renewal feature is disabled, and authorises recurring payments. The auto-renewal clause then defines the length of what comes next: renewal happens at the end of each subscription period for a subsequent period whose length is equal to the most recent subscription period before renewal, or the initial subscription period, or any shorter period then available for purchase. For the plan sold on the deal page, a 48-month term renews for another 48-month term unless something is changed.\n\nThe clause also fixes when the money moves. The provider charges the payment method before the end of the current subscription period, described in the terms as from 30 to 0 calendar days before it. On a 48-month term the earliest charge point therefore sits at about 47 months in, with roughly one month of the paid term still to run - derived from the published 48-month term and the published 30-to-0-day charge window. If the charge fails at that date, the terms say further attempts may follow until the current period ends.

sections.heading: The email you are promised is optional
sections.body:
On notice, the terms are candid. The provider has the right, but not an obligation, to inform the buyer by email about an upcoming auto-renewal before the charge date, and the clause gives the example that customers on one-month subscriptions will not be informed. In contractual terms the notice floor is zero days, and 30 days is the ceiling the charge window allows, not a commitment.

The same clause places the duty on the account holder: it is the buyer's sole responsibility to modify and maintain account settings, including setting renewal options and keeping the payment method current and valid, and the provider states it is not liable for an interruption or loss of service that follows from a failure to do so. There is also an account-updater provision under which the provider may, but is not obliged to, accept updated card details from the card issuer and apply them automatically.

Read together with the previous section, the arrangement is: the renewal is automatic, the term length is the same as the one just bought, the charge can land 30 days before the end, and the reminder is discretionary.

sections.heading: The renewal rate on the card is not a locked price
sections.body: The deal page prints $25.99/mo when you renew against a promotional rate of $7.99/mo, a step of 3.25x derived from those two printed figures and covered in more detail in this site's article on the first-term and renewal split. The terms make clear that the printed renewal figure is a display, not a cap. The change-of-fees clause reserves the right to change or modify fees, expressly including the renewal fees displayed at the site at the time of the first purchase, at any time and without need for further notice, with the change taking effect when the service comes up for renewal, and states that continuing to use the services after the change takes effect counts as acceptance. The auto-renewal clause says the same from the other side: the fees charged at renewal may be higher or lower than the fees for the initial or most recent subscription period.\n\nSo the number on the card answers the question what will I pay if nothing changes, and the terms answer the question what am I promised, which is a rate the provider may move at renewal without a further notice.

sections.heading: Buying a new promotional plan instead of renewing does not convert the old one
sections.body:
The obvious workaround - let the plan lapse and buy the promotional price again - is addressed by the provider in a dedicated support article. Purchasing a new plan creates a separate service rather than extending an existing one; hosting plans cannot be merged, and content is not moved automatically between them for free. The article recommends renewing the original plan instead, to avoid manual work and downtime. The promotional price is attached to a new service, not to the service already running.

The other routes have walls too. The upgrade article states that a web or cloud hosting plan cannot be upgraded directly to a VPS and that a VPS must be bought separately with the content migrated manually; that Agency hosting does not support direct upgrades and requires buying a separate Agency plan and moving sites with the clone tool; and that moving to an Agency plan changes the IP address. Downgrading works differently again: it is done from the dashboard, and if the option is enabled the buyer may change the billing cycle and select a refund method, which means a downgrade - unlike a cancellation - can carry money back.

One warning applies to every route. The cancel-service article states that terminating a service, whether by expiration or by refund, permanently deletes all of its associated data, and recommends downloading a manual backup of website files, databases and email first.

sections.heading: How to read the exit before you buy
sections.body:
Six questions separate the advertised exit from the contractual one, and all six can be answered from pages the provider publishes.

First: does the guarantee end the service or pause it? Here it ends it, immediately. Second: what exactly falls inside the guarantee period, and are there shorter clocks for any part of the order - in this case 96 hours for a general-TLD registration and 7 days for a Brazilian one, against 30 days for the hosting plan itself. Third: is there any published pro-rata after the window closes? Here there is not; the terms default to non-refundable fees and charge the chosen period upfront. Fourth: does the plan renew by itself, and for how long? Here it does, for a period equal in length to the term just bought. Fifth: when is the renewal charge taken, and what notice is promised before it? Here from 30 to 0 days before the end, with notice described as a right and not an obligation. Sixth: is the renewal rate on the card a promise? Here it is a displayed rate that the change-of-fees clause allows the provider to move at renewal without further notice.

A deal that prints risk-free and Cancel anytime is not necessarily misleading; it is answering a different question from the one a buyer is asking. The advertised exit is the 30-day window. The contractual exit is the renewal switch, and it decides only whether the next term happens.
