title: Cloud hosting deals sell 24/7 support in five phrases. Only one comes with a number.
description: The same Priority 24/7 expert support badge is printed on a $2.99 plan and a $29 plan. The only response time published anywhere is a one-minute median, on live chat, in English.
answer: The deal pages sell support with five different phrases - 24/7 support, 24/7 customer support, Priority 24/7 expert support, 24/7 priority support and 24/7 Customer Success support - and exactly one of them carries a number. The cloud-hosting FAQ publishes a median response time of one minute for requests in English, on live chat. That is a median rather than a ceiling, it is attached to one channel in one language, and it is the only response-time figure printed on any of the six pages read for this guide. The provider's contractual document points the other way: the customer service policy, last revised 2023-05-10, promises live chat only as soon as possible, with no number at all, and attaches its single figure - within 1 business day - to the email and ticket route instead. The same four-word badge, Priority 24/7 expert support, is printed on the $2.99/mo Premium card, the $3.99/mo Unlimited card, the $7.99/mo Cloud Startup card and the $29/mo Agency card, and as a row in the compare-plans table. The word priority is defined on one page only, the cloud-hosting FAQ, where it means routing to cloud-hosting experts instead of the general Customer Success specialists. VPS plan cards print no support badge at all.
unique_note: Sourced facts: every quoted phrase, price, count and date comes from the six provider pages listed at the bottom of this page, read on 2026-10-02; the plan-card support strings, the FAQ answer, the customer service policy wording, the contact-page wording and the page-title strings are quoted as printed. Derived, and labelled as derived wherever it appears: the count of distinct support phrases, the mapping of each phrase to the page that prints it, the observation that one badge string covers four price points, the comparison between the policy's last-revised stamp and the contact page's updated stamp, and the note that a median leaves half of requests slower by definition. Reported as unstated rather than estimated: any response time for a language other than English, any response time for email, ticket or WhatsApp, any per-plan channel entitlement, and any figure at all in the contractual document for the live-chat route. No benchmark domain was read for this article; the benchmark domain recorded in the gap table is blocked from this machine and was not fetched.

sections.heading: The support badge, exactly as printed
sections.body:
The pricing page prints one support string on every plan card, and it is the same four words every time: Priority 24/7 expert support. The string appears nine times on that page, including once as a row in the compare-plans table.

Here is each plan card with the exact support string it carries and the price printed beside it:

Premium - $2.99/mo on the 48-month term, renews at $10.99/mo - Priority 24/7 expert support
Unlimited - $3.99/mo, renews at $16.99/mo - Priority 24/7 expert support
Cloud Startup - $7.99/mo, renews at $25.99/mo - Priority 24/7 expert support
Agency - $29/mo on a 24-month term, $49/mo when it renews - Priority 24/7 expert support

The same page carries a different badge in its header strip, where it sits beside the money-back guarantee and the cancellation promise: 30-day money-back guarantee, 24/7 support, Cancel anytime. So the page uses 24/7 support at the top and Priority 24/7 expert support on the cards below it.

The all-plans-include list is thinner still - Reliable hosting, Custom domain, Email, Building tools - and does not mention support at all.

sections.heading: Five phrases for one benefit
sections.body:
Across the three product pages read for this guide, support is sold under five distinct phrases. These are the strings as printed, and the page that prints each one:

24/7 support - the header badge on the pricing page, once, and again in the Fully managed block on the cloud page
24/7 customer support - the hero strip on the cloud page, once
Priority 24/7 expert support - the plan cards and the compare-plans table on the pricing page, nine times, plus the cloud feature list, once
24/7 priority support - the cloud FAQ sentence that lists what every cloud package includes, once
24/7 Customer Success support - the cloud-versus-VPS comparison answer on the VPS page, once

Not one of those five phrases is accompanied by a contact channel, a language, a plan tier or a response time on the page that prints it. The words are the whole claim.

The VPS page is the outlier. Its plan cards print no support string at all: the phrase priority support appears zero times and 24/7 support appears zero times on that page, even though its own FAQ tells buyers that Customer Success agents can be reached via live chat 24/7 and its comparison answer refers to 24/7 Customer Success support.

sections.heading: The one number, and the three qualifiers attached to it
sections.body:
The only response-time figure printed anywhere in this set of pages sits in a single FAQ answer on the cloud page, under the question What does expert priority support mean? The answer reads:

With priority support, your questions will go straight to our cloud hosting experts, instead of the general Customer Success specialists. These technical agents know the ins and outs of cloud hosting, which means you will get more accurate answers, faster. Our priority support is available 24/7 via live chat, with a median response time of one minute for requests in English.

Three qualifiers travel with that number. It is a median, which by definition means half of the requests measured were slower than one minute. It is attached to live chat and to no other channel. And it is stated for requests in English only.

The same answer immediately offers 10 other languages, including Spanish, French, Portuguese, Chinese and Arabic, and attaches no figure to any of them.

The definition of the word priority is also only here. On this page it describes routing - your question goes to cloud-hosting experts rather than to the general Customer Success specialists - and the page's own wording confirms that the general specialists are the normal destination. It is a queue claim, not a longer opening window. The phrase median response time appears once on the cloud page and zero times on the pricing page, the VPS page, the customer service policy and the contact page.

sections.heading: The contract puts its only number on a different channel
sections.body:
The provider's contractual document on support is the customer service policy, and it answers the question differently. Under the heading How we handle Customer Service it lists exactly two routes.

Live chat: From your account or from the Help Center. We will reply as soon as possible.
Email/Ticket system: Sending an email message to support@hostinger.com. We will reply within 1 business day.

The only reply-time figure in the document - within 1 business day - belongs to the email and ticket route, which no deal page mentions. The route that carries the FAQ's one-minute median, live chat, has no number in the policy at all: as soon as possible.

Counting the policy's own words makes the split plain. The string 24/7 appears zero times in it. The phrase response time appears zero times. The phrase 1 business day appears once. Live chat appears three times, twice of them inside a security warning that the deal pages never carry, which strictly prohibits sharing sensitive information such as passwords, full credit-card details or copies of ID documents in live chat and states that doing so is entirely at the customer's own risk.

The policy is stamped Last revised: 2023-05-10, more than three years before this guide was written.

sections.heading: The route the deal pages never name
sections.body:
The page that actually documents how to reach support describes a route the deal pages do not name. Under the heading How to contact Hostinger support, updated one week before this guide was written, the first instruction is: The fastest way to get help is through Hostinger dashboard. The mechanism is an Ask AI button at the top of any dashboard page, and clicking it opens a chat with Hostinger Agent, described on the page as the provider's AI assistant that replaced Kodee.

The page lists what that assistant can do: answer common questions, guide a user through troubleshooting steps, provide relevant help articles, help clarify error messages, and perform selected account actions after the user confirms the request. On Business Web and Cloud hosting plans it can also perform WordPress admin actions directly from the chat.

A human is conditional, not the default. The page says: If additional assistance is needed, a Customer Success Specialist can join the chat to continue helping you. It also offers a WhatsApp tab that continues the same conversation, including voice notes and scheduled job results.

The word counts on this page are the sharpest evidence of the gap. Hostinger Agent appears 27 times. WhatsApp appears five times. The phrase live chat appears zero times. The word ticket appears zero times. The string 24/7 appears zero times. The page that documents support does not use the vocabulary the deal pages sell, and it never mentions a ticket route at all - even though the contractual policy's single reply-time figure is attached to one.

sections.heading: Two smaller mismatches that cut against the badge
sections.body: First, the support center's own page title reads Hostinger Support Center - Get help and guides 24/7, while the body text of that same page contains the string 24/7 zero times. The 24/7 claim lives in the title tag, not in the page.\n\nSecond, the Agency card is the only plan card in this set that adds anything support-adjacent: Proactive monitoring alerts, marked NEW. No other card differentiates its support from any other card, which is the point - the badge is identical at $2.99/mo and at $29/mo.

sections.heading: The support table a buyer cannot find on the site
sections.body:
Putting the printed strings beside the published figures produces the table the site does not publish. Unstated cells are reported as unstated, not filled in.

Premium, $2.99/mo - printed string: Priority 24/7 expert support - channel named: unstated - language named: unstated - response figure: unstated
Unlimited, $3.99/mo - printed string: Priority 24/7 expert support - channel named: unstated - language named: unstated - response figure: unstated
Cloud Startup, $7.99/mo - printed string: Priority 24/7 expert support - channel named: unstated - language named: unstated - response figure: unstated
Agency, $29/mo - printed string: Priority 24/7 expert support - channel named: unstated - language named: unstated - response figure: unstated
VPS plans - printed string: none - channel named: live chat, in the FAQ only and never on the card - language named: unstated - response figure: unstated
Cloud hosting as a product - printed string: 24/7 priority support - channel named: live chat - language named: English only - response figure: median one minute
All plans, contractual - printed string: not applicable - channel named: live chat and email/ticket - language named: unstated - response figure: 1 business day on email/ticket, unstated on live chat

The only cell in that table that contains a number is a product-level FAQ answer, not a plan-card claim. No plan card in this set names the channel its badge entitles the buyer to, and no page maps a tier to a channel.

sections.heading: What this means before you buy
sections.body:
Four things follow for anyone reading a support badge on a hosting deal.

The badge does not distinguish tiers. The identical string is printed from $2.99/mo to $29/mo, so it cannot be used to compare plans. On these pages it is a constant, not a variable.

The one published number is narrow. It is a median, so it is a midpoint rather than a ceiling; it is stated for live chat; and it is stated for English. If the question will be asked in another language, or sent by email, no figure is published to hold anyone to.

The binding figure is the smaller one on the other channel. The customer service policy promises a reply within 1 business day on email and ticket, and only as soon as possible on live chat. A buyer who wants a documented reply time should read that as the number that actually applies.

The advertised chat now opens with an AI assistant, and a human specialist joins only if additional assistance is needed. That is stated on the provider's own contact page, and it is absent from every deal page and from the 2023-05-10 policy that governs support.

title: Cloud hosting deals print a monthly price. Five billing rules decide the real bill
description: The deal pages publish a monthly rate and an upfront total, and say nothing about how the money is collected: 46 regional brands with different payment methods, a currency fixed at registration, installments on 4 of those brands, a whole-term upfront charge and a 30-day expired-plan window.
answer: The deal pages publish a monthly rate, a billing term and an upfront total, and nothing about how the money is actually collected. On the cloud hosting page the words PayPal, installment, currency and card appear zero times. On the pricing page the word payment appears once, and it describes an ecommerce plan's own store checkout rather than how the customer pays the provider. The provider meanwhile publishes 46 regional brands with different payment methods and different currencies, states that an account's currency is fixed at registration and that support cannot override it, publishes an installment option on only 4 of those 46 brands, charges the whole term upfront, and does not allow renewal periods to be stacked. A missed payment is not a suspension with a grace period: it puts the plan into Expired status for 30 days, and reactivating it restores website files and databases but not email accounts or their data.
unique_note: Every figure and quotation on this page is taken from the pages listed under Sources, read on 3 October 2026. The counts of how often a word appears on the two deal pages, the count of regional brands, the number of brands publishing installments and the number listing crypto payments are derived by this site from those pages' own text. The per-brand payment methods, the currency rule, the installment terms, the upfront-charge rule, the non-stackable renewal rule and the 30-day expired-plan window are quoted from the provider's published pages. Where arithmetic is used it is labelled as derived in the sentence that uses it. Anything the provider does not publish is reported as unstated, never estimated.

sections.heading: What the deal pages print about paying, counted
sections.body:
The starting point is a word count, because it is the cleanest way to show what the deal pages leave out. On the cloud hosting page, the strings PayPal, installment, currency and card each appear zero times. On the pricing page, the same four strings appear zero times, and the word payment appears once.

That single mention is not about paying the provider at all. It sits inside the description of the ecommerce plan and reads that the plans include inventory management, multiple payment methods and 0% transaction fees. It is a feature of the store a customer might build on the hosting, not a statement about how the hosting is bought.

What the pages do print about money is the price and its boundaries. The pricing page carries the line Prices are listed without VAT in its footer. The cloud hosting page goes further and states that the price displayed is the monthly rate excluding applicable taxes, and that the total price for the plan to be paid upfront at checkout includes the monthly rate multiplied by the number of months in the plan, along with any applicable taxes.

So the deal page is precise about the size of the number and silent about the pipe it travels through. Which methods are accepted, in which currency, whether the amount can be split, when the money leaves the account and what happens if it does not are all answered somewhere else.

sections.heading: The payment rail is chosen by region, not by the plan
sections.body:
The provider's own payment-methods page opens by saying that the available payment methods and currency options vary depending on the brand where the services are purchased, and names Hostinger Global, Hostinger India and Hostinger France as examples. The page then lists the methods brand by brand. Counting the brand entries on that page gives 46.

Those 46 entries are not 46 variations on one list. Card networks differ: the global brand lists Visa, MasterCard, Amex, Discover, JCB, DinersClub and Maestro, while the Mexican brand lists Visa, MasterCard, Amex and Carnet, and the Brazilian brand adds Elo, HiperCard, Aura and Mercado Libre. Wallets differ too. Of the 46 brands, 41 list PayPal and 22 list Apple Pay. The global brand lists PayPal, Apple Pay, Google Pay and AliPay as its wallets.

The most widely repeated line on the page is crypto. 39 of the 46 brands carry the phrase Crypto payments. That is a derived count from the page's own entries, and it is worth stating plainly because a buyer comparing two deals will not find it on either deal page.

Two further rules sit in the notes at the top of the same page. Funds already in the Hostinger balance are automatically applied as a discount to the next invoice. And adding an eligible payment method to the account is what allows the services to renew automatically, which means the payment rail and the auto-renewal behaviour are the same decision.

sections.heading: The currency is decided once, at registration, and cannot be changed
sections.body:
This is the rule with the longest shadow. The provider states that it is not possible to change the currency of an existing Hostinger account, and that to use a different currency a customer must create a new Hostinger account using a different email address on the specific local brand website that supports that currency.

A dedicated support page explains why. The account currency is determined by the specific regional brand selected during initial registration, and that setting is permanent and cannot be altered once the account is created. Each regional brand operates as an independent legal and financial entity with its own localized pricing, tax structures and payment processors, so the currency cannot be changed or transferred to another regional billing system afterwards. The page is explicit that this is not a policy a human can waive: the currency is fixed at account creation and tied to the regional brand's billing system, and support agents cannot override the limitation.

The page offers four example mappings: the global brand bills in United States dollars, the Indian brand in Indian rupees, the Brazilian brand in Brazilian reals and the French brand in euros, and notes that the provider offers more than 40 regional locations. Local payment methods follow the same boundary. UPI is named as available on the Indian brand and PIX on the Brazilian brand, and the page warns that if a specific local payment method is unavailable after choosing the respective location, it may not be currently supported.

The practical consequence is that the currency is part of the purchase, not a display setting. A buyer who registers on one brand and later wants to be billed in another currency has one documented route: open a second account with a different email. The same page notes that if the old account holds active services it cannot be deleted, that domain names can be moved to the new account, and that other services can be refunded if eligible or else kept until they expire with auto-renewal disabled.

sections.heading: Installments exist on 4 of the 46 brands, and are hidden by default
sections.body:
Splitting the payment is possible, but only on a small slice of the map. Of the 46 brand entries on the payment-methods page, 4 publish an installment line: Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico. The installments page confirms the boundary from the other direction, stating that installment payments are available across several LATAM brands for purchases made with a credit card, and that the option is only available on the brands listed. PIX, Boleto and debit cards do not support installments, only credit cards do.

The published ceilings differ by brand: up to 12 months in Argentina and Brazil, up to 36 months in Colombia, and 3, 6, 9 or 12 months in Mexico. Every one of those four entries adds that availability and interest rates can depend on the buyer's bank.

The option is also not offered by default. The provider states that the installment option is not shown by default at checkout, and that a saved credit card must be deleted first, under the billing and payment-methods area of the dashboard, because the system otherwise defaults to charging the card in full. Automatic renewal must also be switched off, under the subscriptions area. Only then does choosing the other-payment-methods route at checkout and entering card details reveal the installment choices.

Two further conditions matter. Once a payment has been completed in full as a single charge it cannot be converted to installments afterwards, although support can open a request to reissue the invoice. And on interest the page is careful: the price shown on a plan page in the form of a monthly multiple reflects the provider's base charge split across that many months before any fees, the provider itself does not charge interest, and the buyer's financial institution may add interest on top, which is why the final per-installment amount can be slightly higher at checkout.

sections.heading: The monthly rate is not the amount charged
sections.body:
Three separate published statements say the headline figure is not the number that hits the card.

First, the upfront rule. The provider states that the full amount for the selected subscription period is charged upfront, and that longer billing cycles usually provide a lower average monthly price. The monthly figure is a division, not a schedule.

Second, the deal page's own caveat, already quoted above: the total to be paid upfront at checkout includes the monthly rate multiplied by the number of months, along with any applicable taxes, and the price displayed excludes those taxes.

Third, a support page written specifically for the mismatch. It lists the reasons a payment may reflect a different amount on the payment method than the cart or invoice showed, and the first reason it gives is paying in installments, where the financial institution's interest is added.

The dashboard invoice and the card statement are therefore two different documents by design. The provider's own installments page states that the dashboard invoice always shows the base price of the service, without the interest added by the financial institution, while the card invoice reflects the amount charged by the bank. The final amount, including all fees, is shown at checkout before the purchase is confirmed.

sections.heading: Renewal periods cannot be stacked, and only the first term carries the deal
sections.body:
Two rules decide the shape of the second payment. The provider states that subscriptions are paid upfront for the selected billing cycle, that renewing early extends the service from the current expiration date, and that renewal periods cannot be stacked beyond the next billing term, so multiple renewals cannot be combined into one accumulated period.

The available periods are published per product: one month, 12 months, 24 months or 48 months for web hosting, cloud hosting and business email; one month, 12 months or 24 months for KVM VPS hosting; one month for legacy OpenVZ VPS hosting; and one month or 12 months for Agency hosting. Domains have a minimum renewal period of one year, with some extensions allowing multi-year renewal up to two or three years depending on the registry.

The second rule is the one that decides the price of that second term. On the billing-cycle page the provider states plainly that all billing cycles after initial purchase are billed at regular rate. The promotional rate is a first-term rate. The same page also notes that switching from a monthly to a yearly hosting plan does not qualify for a free domain, and that when the billing cycle is changed as part of a hosting upgrade only the current billing period or 12 months can be selected. If a renewal invoice has already been issued it must be paid before the billing period can be modified, and if the service is manually renewed before its scheduled renewal date only the current billing cycle can be used.

One further restriction is easy to miss because it is about a legacy product: OpenVZ VPS plans support monthly billing only and cannot be changed.

sections.heading: What a missed payment actually does to the site and the mailboxes
sections.body:
The deal pages sell the purchase. The expired-plan page describes the failure, and its boundaries are narrower than a buyer might assume.

A plan that expires because of a missed payment shows an Expired status, and the provider states that it can be reactivated directly from the dashboard home page within 30 days of the expiration date. Renewing restores the websites, and the page confirms that websites created with the provider's AI builder are included in that restoration. Restoration typically takes between 30 minutes and a few hours, depending on the total size of the websites.

Email is the exception. The same page states that email accounts and their data are not included in this restoration process. A buyer whose deal bundles free mailboxes per website, and who lets a payment slip, should read that sentence twice: the websites come back and the mail does not.

There is also a closing door inside the 30 days. The option to download the most recent backup of files and databases is available only while the hosting plan is in Expired status, which lasts for 30 days following the expiration date. Once a hosting plan is fully cancelled after that 30-day window, backups are no longer available and the option no longer appears in the dashboard. The backup itself covers files and databases for HTML and PHP-based websites and does not include emails.

The practical reading is that the only published safety net is a 30-day window with a website-only restore. There is no published grace period before the Expired status begins, no published late-payment fee and no published guarantee that a mailbox can be recovered at all.

sections.heading: The comparison this leaves open
sections.body:
Putting the printed deal beside the published rail produces a small set of derived ratios and a larger set of blanks. The ratios are arithmetic on the counts above and are labelled as such.

Installments are published on 4 of 46 brands, or about 8.7%. Crypto payments appear on 39 of 46, or about 84.8%. PayPal appears on 41 of 46, or about 89.1%.

The reactivation window can be set against the term being sold. On the cloud hosting page the top plan is sold on a 48-month term. Taking four calendar years with one leap day as about 1,461 days, a 30-day reactivation window is roughly 2.05% of the term. A buyer is committing to a period about 49 times longer than the window in which a missed payment can be undone without losing the mailboxes.

The blanks are as important. The provider does not publish a per-plan payment-method list, so a buyer cannot know from the deal page whether the card in their wallet is accepted on the brand they are looking at. It does not publish whether installment options exist for the global dollar brand, and the four brands that do publish them are all regional. It does not publish a grace period between a failed charge and the Expired status. It does not publish the renewal price that will apply at the end of the term, only the rate that applies now and a statement that later cycles bill at regular rate. And it does not publish what happens to mailbox data after the 30-day window closes, beyond the statement that email is excluded from the restore.

None of that makes the deal dishonest. It does mean the deal page answers a narrower question than the one a buyer is asking. The page answers what the hosting costs. It does not answer what paying for it involves, and the difference only becomes visible on the second charge.

sections.heading: Sources and method
sections.body:
Ten provider-published pages were read for this article on 3 October 2026: the pricing page, the cloud hosting page, and eight support articles covering payment methods, installments, the billing cycle, renewal periods and advance payment, the permanent account currency, reactivating an expired plan, being charged a different amount, and managing payment methods. All ten returned HTTP 200 and all are permitted by the provider's robots.txt.

The word counts in the first section were produced by searching the served text of the two deal pages for each string. The brand count of 46 and the counts of 39 crypto, 41 PayPal, 22 Apple Pay and 4 installments were produced by counting the brand entries on the payment-methods page and checking which of them carry each line. No benchmark site was fetched for this article, and no figure here is estimated.

One limitation should be stated. The per-brand lists and the availability of a given local payment method change over time; the provider's own page carries an updated date, and the deal pages carry none. A buyer should treat the deal page's price as the part that is stable and the payment rail as the part that must be re-checked at checkout.

title: Cloud hosting deals badge developer tools without saying which plan unlocks them
description: The cloud plan card prints 18 features and names none of the developer tools. The floors for SSH, staging, cron, Git and the PHP version live in the knowledge base - and they are not one ladder.
answer: On the Cloud Startup card the cloud hosting page sells, 18 feature lines are printed and none of them is staging, SSH, cron jobs or Git deployment. The pricing page does name three of those four - “SSH & WP-CLI for faster site management”, “Free safe staging environments” and “Cron jobs automate tasks” - but it prints them in a block headed “Every plan has everything you need and more”, with no plan tier attached, and the plan comparison underneath has no staging, SSH, cron, Git or PHP-version row at all. The provider's own knowledge base is the only place the floors are stated, and they are not one ladder: SSH needs “Premium Web or greater”, WordPress staging needs “a Business web hosting plan or higher”, a Node.js application needs “a Business web hosting plan or any Cloud hosting plan”, and cron jobs are capped at “a maximum of two” on the Single plan and unlimited from Premium up. Two tools carry product exclusions instead of a tier floor: Git deployment is limited to custom PHP and HTML websites and is excluded from Node.js websites and from AI Builder websites, and the PHP version cannot be changed at all on an account whose only websites were built with AI Builder.
unique_note: Sourced: every eligibility floor, cap, exclusion and warning quoted in this article is printed on one of the ten provider pages listed under Sources - the six knowledge-base articles carry the floors and exclusions, the cloud hosting and pricing pages carry the badge strings and the row lists, and the VPS page carries the root-access language. Derived: the 18-line count on the Cloud Startup card and the counts of how many times each tool name appears on each deal page are my own tallies of the served pages, not provider statements; the statement that the pricing page's comparison carries no staging, SSH, cron, Git or PHP-version row is a reading of that table's own rows; and the statement that the word Business appears on the pricing page only in navigation and footer text rather than as one of the three compared plans is a count of that page's own text. Unstated by every page read: what staging, SSH, cron or Git cost beyond the plan price; whether a staging environment consumes inodes, disk or a website slot; and which of the three plans the pricing page compares satisfies the Business floor that the staging and Node.js articles name.

sections.heading: What the two deal pages actually print
sections.body:
Two pages carry the deal claims here: the cloud hosting page, which sells the Cloud Startup plan this site tracks, and the pricing page, which carries the plan comparison.

The Cloud Startup card prints 18 feature lines: 10 Web Apps, 4 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM, 100 GB NVMe storage, 2 000 000 inodes, 100 PHP workers, unlimited websites, access sharing, a free domain for 1 year, unlimited SSL, 15 vibe coding credits, unlimited mailboxes per website for 1 year, managed hosting for WordPress and WooCommerce and Web Apps, CDN included, a dedicated IP address, priority 24/7 expert support, a 30-day money-back guarantee, and AI SEO ready.

Counting that same page's text for the four tools a developer is most likely to look for returns zero: the cloud hosting page contains the strings staging, SSH, cron and Git zero times each.

The card ends with a link labelled View all features, which is the page telling the reader that the list above it is not the whole list.

On the pricing page the same four strings behave differently: staging, SSH and cron appear twice each, and Git appears zero times.

sections.heading: The block that names three tools and attaches no tier
sections.body:
The pricing page's developer-tool claims sit in a single block, headed Every plan has everything you need and more, listing nine items: SSH & WP-CLI for faster site management, SFTP account management for secure team access, PHP version management offers better performance, Free safe staging environments, 1-click website cloning, Redirects Manager preserves SEO, Cron jobs automate tasks, Free malware scanning, and Unlimited collaborators.

That block is printed twice on the page, and not one of its nine items carries a plan name, a tick mark, an asterisk or a footnote.

A second, shorter block on the same page is headed All plans include and lists only four things: reliable hosting, a custom domain, email, and building tools. None of the developer tools is in it.

The comparison table that follows is where a reader would expect the tier answers to appear, and it is where they are missing. Its rows run through websites, storage, daily backups, CDN, WordPress, AI Builder credits, Web Apps, free domain, WHOIS privacy, mailboxes per website, free email marketing, priority support, AI tools, AI SEO readiness, uptime guarantee, data centers, automatic migration, SSL, inodes, PHP workers, databases, database size, RAM, CPU cores, bandwidth, a dedicated IP, two AI Builder modes, managed WordPress, and a Node.js frameworks row.

There is no staging row, no SSH row, no cron row, no Git row and no PHP-version row.

sections.heading: SSH: the floor is Premium Web, and the jail is your home directory
sections.body:
The provider's SSH article states its floor in its own words: If your hosting plan is Premium Web or greater, you can access your hosting via SSH.

It then adds a scope limit that no deal page mentions: The SSH access type is restricted to your home directory and below.

The remedy it offers a plan below the floor is an upgrade rather than a workaround: If you have a Single hosting plan and you definitely need SSH access, you can consider upgrading your hosting plan.

The VPS page is the contrast case. It advertises Full root access - Customize and manage your VPS environment with unrestricted administrative control - alongside a Web terminal offering One-click root access, and its FAQ answers Can I install custom software on my virtual server hosting? with Yes. With full root access, you have the freedom to configure your VPS for many purposes.

So the same provider sells shell access three ways: unrestricted on a VPS, enabled but confined to the home directory from Premium Web upward, and unavailable on the entry plan. The cloud plan card names none of the three.

sections.heading: Staging: the floor is Business, and publishing overwrites the live site
sections.body:
The staging article sets a higher floor than SSH: you can create and manage these environments directly from Hostinger dashboard if you have a Business web hosting plan or higher. It repeats the condition under its own Before you start heading: Ensure you have a Business web hosting plan or higher.

It then narrows the scope twice. The Hostinger staging tool creates staging environments for root domains. To set up staging for a subdomain, you must do so manually. And if your domain uses external nameservers, you must manually create an A record for the staging subdomain in your active DNS zone.

The most consequential sentence appears in no deal page: Publishing replaces your live files and database with the staging copy. Any changes made to your live website after the staging environment was created will be overwritten and lost.

The same article points Agency plan owners to a separate guide, so the staging tool described here is not the Agency one.

Derived observation: because publishing replaces files and database together, the only safeguard the article describes is a confirmation window to review before clicking Publish. No export step, backup step or diff of the live site is mentioned.

sections.heading: Cron: the one published per-plan number is a cap
sections.body:
The cron article is the only page of the ten that publishes a per-plan number for a developer tool: For Single hosting - Maximum of two cron jobs, and For Premium hosting and above - Unlimited.

It immediately qualifies the word unlimited with a resource rule rather than a job count: When setting up cron jobs, it is essential to consider both CPU and memory limits. If you need to create a significant number of cron jobs, it's recommended to schedule them avoiding simultaneous runs that could lead to performance issues.

The companion setup article adds two operational facts the deal pages never carry: a job's type is either PHP or Custom, and Cron jobs tasks schedule is based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC+0).

Derived: unlimited here is a cap on the number of entries, not a promise about resources, and the entry plan's ceiling of two jobs against no stated ceiling from Premium up is the widest published tier gap of any tool in this set.

sections.heading: Git deployment: three exclusions and one overwrite warning
sections.body:
Git deployment carries the most published exclusions of any tool here, and it is the one that appears zero times on both deal pages read.

The Git article opens with its scope: Git integration is available for custom PHP and HTML websites hosted on web and cloud hosting plans.

It then excludes three cases by name. This does not apply for Node.js websites, instead please refer to the guide on deploying Node.js from a GitHub repository. Hostinger AI Builder websites do not support Git integration. And Agency Hosting plans support a separate GitHub integration for existing websites, which the article later describes as not supporting GitLab or Node.js full-stack applications.

Setup is OAuth-based with no SSH key setup required, and the root directory defaults to public_html, changeable to any valid directory on the hosting account.

The article's own note is the second overwrite warning in this set: Disconnecting or changing your deployment repository will cause newly deployed files to overwrite existing data in your target directory. Deployment history is published, listing the branch name, commit ID, timestamp and status, and automatic deployments can be paused.

sections.heading: PHP versions: a four-version window and a product exclusion
sections.body:
The PHP article publishes both a supported window and a direction of travel. PHP 8.3 is selected by default for new websites, You can only select PHP versions 8.2 and higher up to PHP 8.5, and Older PHP versions (8.1 and below) are no longer available as options.

Downgrades are blocked. For existing websites with older PHP versions, your current PHP version remains active and you can upgrade to any higher PHP version, but Downgrading to lower versions is not possible - with a temporary exception through the website's .htaccess file that the article asks you to revert as soon as you are ready.

The article's closing note is a product exclusion rather than a tier floor: The selected version will apply to all the websites added to your hosting plan (except for websites created using Hostinger AI Builder), and The PHP version cannot be changed if you only have websites created with Hostinger AI Builder.

The pricing page advertises PHP version management offers better performance in its un-tiered block, without mentioning the AI Builder exclusion the knowledge base states - an exclusion that removes the control rather than gating it behind a plan.

sections.heading: Node.js applications: two floors, depending on the product family
sections.body:
The Node.js overview splits the answer three ways by product family. On web or cloud hosting: If you have a Business web hosting plan or any Cloud hosting plan, you can deploy a Node.js application from a GitHub repository or using the file upload method. On a VPS: by using the CloudPanel template on your VPS, you can easily set up and manage Node.js applications, which the page frames as the option for precise control over runtime versions, system dependencies, and deployment workflows. On Agency: If you have a Hostinger Agency plan, you can host Node.js projects as static front-end applications.

The cloud hosting page's own FAQ gives the short version - Our Cloud and Shared Business Plan hosting plans support Node.js - and the pricing page's comparison carries a Node.js frameworks row, which makes this the one developer tool in the set that the comparison acknowledges.

Derived: the floors collected here are not one ladder. SSH starts at Premium Web, staging at Business, a Node.js application on shared hosting at Business or any Cloud plan; Git is scoped by website type rather than by tier; and cron is capped only on the Single plan.

sections.heading: The six floors side by side, and what is still unstated
sections.body:
Read together, the ten pages produce the comparison below. Every floor, cap, scope limit and exclusion is quoted from the pages named in Sources; the arrangement is mine.

SSH - floor: Premium Web or greater. Scope: restricted to your home directory and below. Source: the SSH article.
WordPress staging - floor: a Business web hosting plan or higher. Scope: root domains only, manual A record with external nameservers. Warning: publishing replaces live files and database. Source: the staging article.
Cron jobs - cap: a maximum of two on Single, unlimited from Premium up. Qualifier: subject to CPU and memory limits. Schedule basis: UTC+0. Source: the two cron articles.
Git deployment - scope: custom PHP and HTML websites on web and cloud hosting. Exclusions: Node.js websites, AI Builder websites, and Agency plans limited to a separate GitHub-only integration. Source: the Git article.
PHP version - window: 8.2 to 8.5, with 8.3 by default. Direction: upgrade only, no downgrade. Exclusion: not changeable on an AI Builder-only account. Source: the PHP article.
Node.js application - floor: a Business web hosting plan or any Cloud hosting plan. Alternatives: VPS via the CloudPanel template, or Agency as static front-end only. Source: the Node.js article.

Still unstated by every page read: what staging, SSH, cron or Git cost, if anything, beyond the plan price; whether a staging environment consumes inodes, disk or a website slot; and which of the three plans the pricing page compares - Premium, Unlimited and Cloud Startup - satisfies the Business floor that the staging and Node.js articles name. On the pricing page the word Business appears in navigation and footer text, not as one of the compared plans.

title: Cloud hosting deals bundle a mailbox free for a year. The provider's own table caps it at 1 GB
description: Plan cards print 2, 10 or unlimited mailboxes per website, free for 1 year, and no storage figure or sending rate. The provider's own email limits table gives the bundled 1-year mailbox 1 GB of storage and 100 messages a day, against 5 GB and 1,000 a day on the cheapest paid mailbox.
answer: The plan cards on the two pages this site tracks print a mailbox count and a clock - 2 mailboxes per website on Premium, unlimited on Unlimited and Cloud Startup, 10 on Agency Startup, each labelled free for 1 year - and no storage figure and no sending rate. The provider's own email limits table supplies both: the mailbox included free for a year is a Business Starter trial with a 1 GB storage limit per mailbox and a daily message rate of 100 inbound and 100 outbound. The cheapest paid mailbox, Business Starter at $0.39 per mailbox per month on a 48-month term, is printed at 5 GB and 1,000 a day. That makes the bundled mailbox one fifth of the paid one's storage and one tenth of its daily rate, and the bundled free mailbox cannot buy the 30 GB or 50 GB storage add-on that paid mailboxes can - the only published route to more space is upgrading every mailbox to a paid plan. All limits in that table are per mailbox, and its daily rates run over a rolling 24 hours. Every figure above is copied from a provider page; the ratios between them are arithmetic on those printed numbers and are labelled as derived below.
unique_note: This page quotes figures printed on the provider's own pages and links to each one. The 1 GB storage limit, the 100 messages a day, the 5 GB and 1,000 a day on Business Starter, the 30-day trial's 10 GB, the 10 per minute and 100 per day on unauthenticated PHP mail, the 50 MB, 35 MB and 25 MB message size caps, the 30 GB and 50 GB add-on packages and the 48-month totals are all quoted as printed. Everything labelled derived is arithmetic on those printed figures: the one-fifth and one-tenth ratios, the messages-per-hour conversions, the number of maximum-size messages a 1 GB mailbox holds, the share of the 48-month term the 1-year entitlement covers, and the newsletter comparison. No storage figure, sending rate, mailbox count, price or duration has been estimated, and cells the provider does not publish are reported as unstated.

sections.heading: What the plan cards print, and what they leave out
sections.body:
The pricing page prints a mailbox line on every plan card, in the same block, under the same two-word label. Premium, at $2.99 a month on a 48-month term, prints 2 mailboxes per website - free for 1 year. Unlimited, at $3.99, prints unlimited mailboxes per website - free for 1 year. Cloud Startup, at $7.99, prints unlimited mailboxes per website - free for 1 year. Agency Startup, at $29 a month on a 24-month term, prints 10 mailboxes per website - free for 1 year.

The cloud hosting page repeats the same construction on the plan this site tracks - unlimited mailboxes per website - free for 1 year - and its FAQ summarises the bundle as a free domain, free ssl certificates, free domain-based emails, and 24/7 priority support. So the card answers two questions: how many mailboxes, and for how long. It never answers the third: how much mail one of those mailboxes holds, or how much it may send.

That absence is measurable rather than rhetorical. The word mailbox appears 11 times on the pricing page and once on the cloud hosting page, and the word email 20 and 9 times respectively. The GB values that do appear on the pricing page sit beside hosting storage, RAM and VPS resource lines - 20 GB SSD, 50 GB NVMe, 100 GB NVMe, 12 GB of RAM, 300 GB NVMe - and not beside the mailbox line. Neither deal page prints a per-mailbox gigabyte.

sections.heading: The provider's own limits table is where the number lives
sections.body:
The provider publishes a separate article titled Parameters and limits of Hostinger Mail. It splits email into three things the deal page treats as one: Business Email plans, which it calls standalone, professional email services; a Business Email Free Trial, described as a trial period of professional email included with select hosting or domain purchases; and Free Business Email, described as legacy email versions bundled with specific web hosting plans and marked as no longer offered since April 2025.

The card's free for 1 year matches the second of those. The article states that the 1-year trial is included with specific hosting plans, and that the mailboxes per domain vary per hosting plan - which is why plan cards can print different counts for what is nominally the same product. It then publishes the trial's own row: a storage limit of 1 GB, a daily message rate of 100 inbound and 100 outbound, and 10 AI credits in total. Everything else, it says, matches the full Business Starter plan.

The same table gives the 30-day trial - the one available through selected domain purchases, which includes 1 mailbox - a storage limit of 10 GB. Both trials share the same 100-a-day message rate. So the trial attached to a domain purchase holds ten times what the trial attached to a hosting plan holds.
Derived from the printed figures: 10 GB divided by 1 GB is 10.

sections.heading: The paid mailbox the table prices the upgrade against
sections.body:
The same table prices the three standalone plans the product page sells. Business Starter is 5 GB of storage and 1,000 messages a day. Business Standard is 20 GB and 3,000 a day. Business Premium is 50 GB and 3,000 a day. All three print unlimited mailboxes per domain, advanced spam and antivirus protection, custom DKIM, and a 100-recipient cap per message.

The email product page prints the prices per mailbox: $0.39, $0.99 and $1.99 a month on a 48-month term, renewing at $1.59, $2.79 and $3.99. Each card says Price per mailbox, for 48-month term, and each includes 1 mailbox.

Set the bundled free mailbox beside the cheapest paid one and the gap is arithmetic. Derived from the printed figures: 1 GB against 5 GB is one fifth, and 100 messages a day against 1,000 is one tenth. The free mailbox holds a fifth of the storage and may send a tenth of the messages of a mailbox costing $0.39 a month on the same 48-month term.

The message limit row sharpens the point. Paid plans print 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000 message units. The bundled trial's message limit is not published at all, so the table leaves that cell blank for the mailbox the deal gives away.

sections.heading: The free mailbox cannot buy its way out of 1 GB
sections.body:
Paid mailboxes have a published escape hatch. The provider sells a Flexible Storage Add-on in 30 GB or 50 GB packages. It can be purchased once per domain, follows the same renewal cycle as the email plan, is paid upfront, and the extra space can be split across mailboxes in 1 GB steps. A single mailbox cannot be pushed above 100 GB in total, the storage can only be allocated within the domain where it was bought, and the article states that additional storage is non-refundable.

The bundled free mailbox is excluded from all of it. The add-on article states plainly that the Flexible Storage Add-on is not available for Free Email plans, and that to increase storage for Free Email you need to upgrade all mailboxes to a Business Email plan. The limits table lists the add-on as available for all three paid plans.

Two more rules close the door on mixing the two. Creating a mailbox requires either an active hosting plan eligible for a free email trial or a standalone mail plan, and the mailbox article notes that if you purchase a paid email plan during setup, the free trial becomes unavailable for that domain, because only one email order type can be active per domain. The limits article states the same constraint from the other side: it is not possible to combine or setup a free email or free trial with a domain that is already using a paid plan.

Derived from the printed figures: the smallest add-on package, 30 GB, is 30 times the entire storage of the bundled 1 GB mailbox - and that is the one mailbox that cannot buy it.

sections.heading: At 1 GB the ceiling stops inbound mail, not just outbound
sections.body:
The storage article describes what happens as a mailbox fills. Webmail shows a warning banner at 90 per cent full, a more prominent one at 94, and an urgent one at 98. At 100 per cent the banner becomes permanent and cannot be dismissed, and at that point you cannot receive new emails until storage space is freed up or expanded.

Trash does not accumulate indefinitely: messages in Trash are automatically deleted after 30 days. Two housekeeping routes are offered - delete old mail and empty the spam folder, or upgrade the plan and buy more storage. On the bundled free mailbox the second route is closed, which leaves the first.

Three size caps apply to every version of the service, free or paid. An inbound email including attachments may not exceed 50 MB, an outbound email including attachments may not exceed 35 MB, and an outbound attachment may not exceed 25 MB.

Derived from the printed figures: at 1 GB, a single maximum-size inbound message at 50 MB is about 5 per cent of the whole mailbox, so 20 of them would fill it. Twenty-nine maximum-size outbound messages at 35 MB would do the same. A mailbox advertised as free for 1 year is a mailbox that 20 large messages can fill.

sections.heading: The sending rate has two published numbers, and they measure different things
sections.body:
The limits table gives the bundled 1-year mailbox a daily message rate of 100 inbound and 100 outbound. It states that all limits in the article apply per individual mailbox rather than per domain or per plan, that each mailbox gets its own full allowance, and that daily rates are calculated over a rolling 24-hour period. It spells out the split: a limit of 100 allows for 100 sent messages and 100 received messages in a 24-hour period.

A separate article on PHP mail publishes a different pair of numbers for a different thing. Sending through unauthenticated functions such as php mail() is capped at 10 emails per minute and 100 emails per day, and the article says that with a Business Starter or Business Premium email you get at least a 10-times higher limit of daily outgoing messages. The provider also ships a rate limit log to the hosting account, updated hourly, recording which mailboxes exceed the limit.

The two pages reconcile. The bundled mailbox's published daily rate of 100 matches the unauthenticated limit of 100 a day, and the paid plan's 1,000 a day in the limits table is exactly the 10-times-higher figure the PHP article describes. Two provider pages, one ratio, and no absolute number published for the free tier beyond 100.

Derived from the printed figures: 100 messages a day is about 4.2 an hour, and 1,000 a day is about 41.7 an hour. A single newsletter to 1,000 opted-in subscribers is ten times the bundled mailbox's entire daily outbound allowance - which is why the plan card carries a separate line for AI email marketing beside the mailbox line rather than folding campaigns into it.

sections.heading: A suspended mailbox loses the dashboard as well as the outbox
sections.body:
The suspension article describes an automated action rather than a manual one. If a mailbox is automatically disabled or shows a Suspended status, it typically means the system has detected suspicious activity or spam originating from the email order, and the suspension applies to one or more mailboxes associated with the domain. While it is in place, you cannot send emails or manage your mailboxes.

Reactivating it is conditional. Before the service can be resumed you must update the passwords for all mailboxes under the affected domain, check the website for malware and protect the contact forms, scan your own devices for malware that might be sending mail through a mail client, and review your sending habits. Only then does the dashboard expose the switch - Emails, then Mailboxes, then the options menu, then Settings, then the Suspend receiving toggle - and the article asks you to wait at least two hours before resuming, so the mail servers can synchronise. If the underlying cause is not fixed, it warns, the email service will get suspended again after you reactivate it.

Putting the two printed statements together: because management access is withdrawn along with sending, a suspension on a 1 GB mailbox is not only an outbound outage - it also removes the dashboard route a customer would use to delete mail and free the space.

sections.heading: The mailbox clock is a quarter of the term you buy
sections.body:
Every card prints free for 1 year. The term being sold on the same page is 48 months: the pricing page prints 48-month totals of $143.52 on Premium, $191.52 on Unlimited and $383.52 on Cloud Startup, and states that all plans are paid upfront and that the monthly rate reflects the total plan price divided by the number of months in the plan.

Derived from the printed figures: 12 months of email entitlement inside a 48-month term covers 25 per cent of the term. The remaining 36 months carry no stated email entitlement on either deal page.

The limits article adds two conditions that decide whether the year even runs its course. If you cancel a Business Email free trial, it cannot be activated again. And if the hosting plan expires before 1 year, the email trial is canceled. Trial limits, it adds, are automatically lifted upon upgrading to a paid plan, and the number of free trials you can claim depends on how many websites your hosting plan supports.

The mailbox article describes how the clock starts. A free email is claimed rather than granted: the customer opens the dashboard, clicks Start Free or Claim free email, picks the domain and confirms. It also notes that a free email can be claimed for any domain you own, even if there is no active website under it, and that hosting plan email limits still apply.

One unit mismatch is left standing. The plan cards count mailboxes per website. The limits article counts mailboxes per domain. Both are printed, neither page reconciles them, and no page states whether a second website on the same plan draws on the same mailbox allowance.

sections.heading: What is still unstated
sections.body:
Several cells the table fills for paid plans are blank for the bundled mailbox. Its message limit in units is not published, while paid plans print 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000. Its storage figure does not appear on either deal page. And no page states what happens to the contents of a mailbox when the 1-year entitlement ends inside a 48-month hosting term - whether mail is retained, frozen or removed.

The mailbox rules themselves are published. A name runs from 1 to 50 characters, may contain letters, numbers and periods, may not contain special characters such as the ampersand, equals sign, underscore, apostrophe, hyphen, plus sign, comma, or angle brackets, and may not contain multiple consecutive periods. A deleted mailbox can be restored within 30 days before permanent deletion.

One further choice is made in the dashboard rather than on the deal page. A web or cloud hosting plan can include Hostinger Email or Titan Email, but not both, and new free email claims through the dashboard only offer Hostinger Email; Titan Email applies only to hosting plans that already had it before November 2025. Which of the two a given plan ships is visible under the plan name in the dashboard, not on the page that sells the plan.

None of this makes the bundled mailbox worthless. It is a real mailbox on the customer's own domain, with its own password and its own storage allotment, reachable through webmail or linkable to an external email client. The point is narrower than that. The card sells a count and a clock, the provider's own table publishes a ceiling of 1 GB and 100 messages a day, and the page that sells the deal prints neither.
